title: Copy List with Random Pointer
description: Brute force to optimized: a hash map from original to copy versus the O(1)-space weave-wire-unweave technique.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

A linked list of length n has each node containing an additional "random" pointer, which could point to any node in the list, or to null. Construct a deep copy of the list: the copy should consist of exactly n brand new nodes, where each new node's value is copied from its original, and both its next and random pointers point to new nodes in the copied list, such that the pointers in the original list and the copied list represent the SAME list state, without either list being affected by the other.

blocks.caption: Weave a copy node right after each original, wire up random pointers using that weaved structure, then unweave

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","The head of a linked list where each node has an extra random pointer (to any node, or null)"],["Output","The head of a completely independent deep copy, with an identical next/random pointer structure"],["Goal","Deep-copy both the next AND random pointer structure, ideally without using O(n) extra map/dictionary space"],["Constraints","0 <= n <= 1000; -10^4 <= Node.val <= 10^4; Node.random is null or points to some node in the list"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Need to copy a \"random\" pointer that can point ANYWHERE in the list, including ahead of the current node","A mapping from original nodes to their copies is the natural first idea (hash map based)"],["An O(1) extra space solution is possible","The \"weave a copy right next to each original\" trick turns the ORIGINAL list itself into a makeshift lookup table, avoiding any separate map"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Every node has two pointers to replicate: next (the usual singly-linked-list pointer) and random (an arbitrary pointer to any node, or null). Both must be correctly replicated in a brand new set of nodes.

blocks.title: Analogy: Copying a Seating Chart With "Buddy" Assignments
blocks.text: Imagine a row of seats (the next pointers) where each seat also has a "buddy" assignment pointing to some other seat in the row (the random pointers). To make an exact copy of both the seating order AND everyone's buddy assignments, one clever trick is to seat each new copy of a person DIRECTLY next to their original, temporarily. That way, "my buddy's copy" is always just "one seat after my buddy," making it trivial to copy the buddy assignments too, before finally splitting the row back into the original seating and the copied seating.

blocks.caption: Weaving interleaves original and copy nodes; unweaving splits them back into two separate, fully independent lists

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: values [7,13,11,10,1], random targets [null, index 0, index 4, index 2, index 0]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Node valued 13 (index 1) has random pointing to index 0 (value 7)","The copy of 13 must also have random pointing to the COPY of 7, not the original","This is exactly what a correct deep copy must replicate"],["Answer","A new list [7,13,11,10,1] with the identical random-pointer index pattern, but made of entirely new nodes","The copy is structurally identical, yet independent"]]}

blocks.text: Example: values [3,3,3], random targets [null, index 0, null]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Only the middle node (index 1) has a random pointer, targeting index 0","The copy must replicate exactly this one random link, and null for the other two","Correctly distinguishes \"has a random pointer\" from \"random is null\""],["Answer","A new list [3,3,3] with only the middle node's random pointer set (to the copy of index 0)","Matches the original's exact random-pointer pattern"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?
Before defaulting to a hash map from original nodes to their copies, notice that physically interleaving each copy right next to its original turns the list itself into a free lookup structure.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The tricky part of this problem is the random pointer, since it can point to a node that has not been created yet (if traversing in order) unless SOME form of lookup from original-node to copy-node is available.

Observation 2: A hash map naturally provides that lookup, but requires O(n) extra space.

Observation 3: Instead, if a copy of each node is inserted DIRECTLY after its original (weaving them together: original1, copy1, original2, copy2, ...), then "the copy of any node X" is always reachable as simply "X.next".

Observation 4: This means node.random's copy is just node.random.next, letting every random pointer be wired up correctly in a single additional pass, with no separate map needed.

Observation 5: A final pass then unweaves the combined list back into two fully separate lists: the original (restored to its original state) and the new deep copy.

This is the "weave, wire, unweave" technique: interleaving copies to create a temporary O(1)-space lookup structure, using it to resolve every random pointer, then splitting the two lists apart again.
6. Brute Force Solution
Use a hash map from each original node to its newly created copy. A first pass creates every copy node (values only); a second pass uses the map to correctly wire up both next and random pointers.
Step by step algorithm

items: First pass: walk the original list, creating one new copy node per original (values only, no pointers yet), storing original-to-copy in a hash map.
Second pass: walk the original list again, using the map to set each copy's next and random pointers to the corresponding COPY nodes (or null).

codes.python:
def copy_random_list(head):
    if not head:
        return None
    mapping = {}                                                            # maps each original node to its brand new copy
    node = head
    while node:
        mapping[node] = Node(node.val)                                     # first pass: create every copy node (values only)
        node = node.next
    node = head
    while node:
        mapping[node].next = mapping.get(node.next)                        # second pass: wire up next and random using the map
        mapping[node].random = mapping.get(node.random)
        node = node.next
    return mapping[head]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n1, n2, n3 = Node(7), Node(13), Node(11)
    n1.next, n2.next = n2, n3
    n2.random = n1
    result = copy_random_list(n1)
    out = []
    node = result
    while node:
        out.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    print(out)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Copy nodes must be created BEFORE any pointer wiring, since a random pointer might target a node that appears later in the list.
The map lookup naturally handles null (using dictionary's .get / getOrDefault-style access), since mapping[null] should also resolve to null, not throw an error.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every original-to-copy relationship is captured correctly by the map, so both next and random pointers always resolve to the correct new nodes.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), two linear passes.
Space: O(n), for the hash map storing every original-to-copy pairing.
Limitation: the O(n) map is avoidable; weaving copies directly into the original list provides the same "lookup" ability using the list structure itself, achieving O(1) extra space.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force needs a hash map purely to answer "given an original node, what is its copy?" Instead, physically place each copy node immediately after its original. Now that question is answered directly by following .next once. A second pass uses this weaved structure to set every random pointer (node.random's copy is node.random.next). A third pass unweaves the combined list back into the original and the copy, fully separated.

Phase 1 (weave): for each original node, create a copy with the SAME value, insert it right after the original, and pull the original's "old next" onto the copy. Phase 2 (wire): for each original node with a non-null random, set original.next.random (the copy) to original.random.next (the copy of the random target). Phase 3 (unweave): walk through, restoring each original's next to skip over its copy, while linking the copies together into their own list.
9. Optimized Solution
Weave copies into the list, wire up random pointers using the weaved structure, then unweave into two independent lists.
Dry run for values [3,3,3], random targets [null, index 0, null]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Phase","Action","State"],"rows":[["1 (weave)","Insert a copy right after each original","3 -> 3' -> 3 -> 3' -> 3 -> 3'"],["2 (wire)","Original index 1's random is index 0; set its copy's random to index 0's copy (index 0.next)","middle 3' .random now points to first 3'"],["3 (unweave)","Split into original list and copy list","Original: 3 -> 3 -> 3 (restored); Copy: 3' -> 3' -> 3' with only the middle one's random set"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The deep copy [3,3,3] correctly has ONLY its middle node's random pointer set (targeting the copy of index 0), matching the original's exact pattern, while the original list is fully restored.

codes.python:
def copy_random_list(head):
    if not head:
        return None

    node = head                                                             # phase 1: weave a copy right after each original node
    while node:
        copy = Node(node.val, node.next)
        node.next = copy
        node = copy.next

    node = head                                                             # phase 2: assign random pointers using the weaved structure
    while node:
        if node.random:
            node.next.random = node.random.next                            # the copy right after node.random IS node.random's copy
        node = node.next.next

    node = head                                                             # phase 3: unweave into two separate lists
    copy_head = head.next
    while node:
        copy = node.next
        node.next = copy.next
        copy.next = copy.next.next if copy.next else None
        node = node.next
    return copy_head


if __name__ == "__main__":
    n1, n2, n3 = Node(7), Node(13), Node(11)
    n1.next, n2.next = n2, n3
    n2.random = n1
    result = copy_random_list(n1)
    out = []
    node = result
    while node:
        out.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    print(out)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), three linear passes over the list.
Space: O(1) extra (excluding the output copy itself, which is required regardless of approach).
Why This Works

While weaved, "the copy of node X" is always exactly X.next, since every copy was inserted directly after its original. This lets phase 2 resolve every random pointer using only pointer-following, no map required. Phase 3 then carefully restores the original list's next pointers (skipping over the interleaved copies) while simultaneously building the copy list's next pointers (skipping over the originals), fully separating the two.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A node's random is null","Its copy's random is correctly left as null, since the wiring step only runs when the original random is non-null"],["A node's random points to itself","node.next.random becomes node.random.next, which is exactly the copy of node itself, correctly handled"],["Empty list (head is null)","Returns null immediately, before any weaving begins"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Phase 1's weaving must preserve "node.next" as the ORIGINAL next (not the copy) when creating each copy node, achieved by reading node.next BEFORE reassigning it.
Phase 2 relies entirely on the weaved structure still being intact, so it must run in full before any unweaving begins.
Phase 3 advances by two nodes at a time on the original side (skipping past each copy), correctly rebuilding both lists in a single final pass.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

When a random/arbitrary pointer needs deep-copying, a hash map from original to copy is the natural first approach; weaving each copy directly next to its original achieves the identical result in O(1) extra space, by turning the list itself into the lookup structure.
Common mistakes

items: Reading node.next AFTER already reassigning it during the weave phase, which loses track of the rest of the original list.
Forgetting to fully restore the original list's next pointers during the unweave phase, leaving it corrupted after the function returns.
Mishandling a null random pointer, accidentally trying to dereference .next on a null value.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Starting with the hash-map approach (simple, clearly correct) before introducing the weave-based O(1)-space optimization mirrors exactly how this problem is meant to be progressively solved in an interview.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Deep copy a list with an EXTRA arbitrary/random pointer" points toward either a hash map (original-to-copy) or the more space-efficient weave-wire-unweave technique.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why is a hash map needed at all (conceptually), even before optimizing? Because a random pointer might target a node that has not been created yet if simply walking the list once in order.

How would you extend this to a doubly linked list with an additional random pointer? The same weave technique still applies, though the "prev" pointers of both lists would also need careful re-wiring during the unweave phase.
What is the exact O(1)-space trick here, in one sentence? Insert each copy directly after its original, temporarily, so "the copy of any node" becomes reachable as simply that node's new .next.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A specialized deep-copy variation of general linked-list traversal techniques, using a "weave a temporary structure into the original" trick that also appears conceptually in some in-place list transformation problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (weave, wire, unweave): O(n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Weave-wire-unweave deep copy
Core Idea: Temporarily interleave a copy right after each original node, so "the copy of any node" is reachable as simply that node's next pointer, resolving random pointers without a separate map
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1) extra
Most Important Observation: Physically placing each copy directly next to its original turns the list itself into a free O(1)-space lookup table
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Weave a copy after each node, wire randoms via node.random.next, then unweave into two lists
